brief.question: Should Legion Capital move 40% of its payment volume (about ₹600 crore a month) from Arvanta Payments to Brevis Pay?

brief.context: Legion Capital Ltd: Fictional RBI-registered NBFC (digital personal and SME loans) with a merchant checkout product, Legion Pay. All payment volume currently goes through Arvanta Payments; Brevis Pay has run a 2% pilot since August 2026.

options.A: Stay with Arvanta Payments for 100% of volume
options.B: Move 40% of volume to Brevis Pay

One-time investment, migration and exit costs
Regulatory compliance: RBI rules, licences, outsourcing norms
Checkout conversion, refunds and payment failures customers feel

payment gateway migration effort
payment success rates and uptime

RBI digital payment regulations

merchant and customer checkout experience
vendor contract terms

positions.summary: Moving 40% volume to Brevis Pay improves overall uptime (99.95% vs 99.82%), p95 latency (1.4s vs 1.9s), and non-weak bank success rates (98.2% vs 97.9%), while resolving Arvanta's worsening settlement ticket delays. However, migration is viable only if Legion uses dynamic bank-level routing to keep underperforming banks (Coral Bank and Tamra Bank, 18% of volume) and unsupported eNACH mandates on Arvanta, and plans for an 8-week implementation timeline given engineering capacity constraints.
handoffs: infosec: Brevis Pay has an open high-severity pen-test finding (missing rate limiting on refund API) open for 47 days (SEC-04).
legal: Arvanta MSA mandates a 90-day written notice period before volume can be reduced (LEG-02).
finance: One-time migration cost is estimated at ₹40 lakh against a ₹4 lakh/month float savings from T+1 settlement (FIN-05, FIN-06).

claims.text: Overall payment success rate is 97.8% on Arvanta over 12 months compared to 97.6% on Brevis Pay during the August–September 2026 pilot.
Brevis Pay significantly underperforms Arvanta at Coral Bank and Tamra Bank (which represent 18% of volume), achieving 94.8% and 95.2% respectively versus Arvanta's 97.5%.
At all other banks representing 82% of payment volume, Brevis Pay outperforms Arvanta with a 98.2% success rate against Arvanta's 97.9%.

By leveraging Legion's payment routing layer to selectively route non-weak banks to Brevis while retaining weak banks (18%) on Arvanta, the blended success rate reaches 98.074%, preventing any success rate drop.
Brevis Pay demonstrates superior system availability and response times, with 99.95% uptime versus Arvanta's 99.82%, and a p95 payment latency of 1,400 ms versus Arvanta's 1,900 ms.

Arvanta experienced 3 major availability incidents in the last 12 months (including a 4-hour outage on 14 June 2026 delaying ₹2.3 crore in collections), whereas Brevis experienced only 1 major incident.
UPI AutoPay mandate success is higher on Brevis (97.4%) than Arvanta (96.1%), though Brevis lacks eNACH support for two small banks covering about 2% of mandates which must remain on Arvanta.

Settlement-delay support complaints against Arvanta have escalated significantly from 120 in July to 340 in September 2026, while Brevis provides real-time settlement and reconciliation APIs and T+1 settlement.

Vendor sales claims that migration can be achieved in under 4 weeks are unverified marketing assertions; internal sizing requires 24 engineer-weeks (6 weeks with 4 engineers), resulting in an 8-week timeline given only 3 available engineers.
Customer complaints for Coral and Tamra Bank rose 40% under Brevis during the pilot, confirming that unconstrained routing to Brevis without bank-level segregation degrades customer experience.
Brevis Pay has an open high-severity penetration test finding regarding missing rate limiting on its refund API that has remained unaddressed for 47 days.

conditions: Traffic routing must exclude Coral Bank and Tamra Bank (18% of volume) and unsupported eNACH mandates (2% of mandates) from Brevis Pay, keeping them on Arvanta Payments via Legion's routing layer.
Migration planning must budget for an 8-week timeline (24 engineer-weeks) utilizing the 3 available payments engineers starting November 2026, rejecting unverified vendor claims of under 4 weeks.
Brevis Pay's open high-severity penetration test vulnerability (missing rate limiting on refund API) must be remediated and verified before going live.

criterion_scores.reason: Arvanta provides consistent multi-bank coverage and a 97.8% baseline success rate, but suffers from lower uptime (99.82%), 3 major outages, and surging settlement operational defects.
Brevis Pay offers superior uptime (99.95%), faster latency (1.4s), and higher mandate and core bank success (98.2%), provided weak banks (18%) and unsupported eNACH (2%) are routed to Arvanta.

positions.summary: Moving 40% of payment volume (₹600 crore/month) to Brevis Pay generates a net monthly recurring benefit of ₹10.4 lakh after accounting for fee savings, India-hosting add-on costs, dispute fee differentials, and float savings. Total one-time costs of ₹65 lakh (₹40 lakh migration plus ₹25 lakh Arvanta exit penalty) achieve payback in 6.25 months, while helping close the ₹3 crore/year payments budget overrun and supporting the board's cost-to-income target.
handoffs: legal: Review whether Arvanta's ₹25 lakh early-exit penalty under §9.2 can be waived or renegotiated, and evaluate commercial exposure from Brevis's 30-day price modification clause and 3-month liability cap.
infosec: Confirm that Brevis Pay's Mumbai region hosting add-on fully satisfies RBI data localization requirements before migration.
ops: Verify engineering team capacity given that 3 available engineers may extend migration from 6 weeks to 8 weeks.

claims.text: Legion Capital processed ₹1,500 crore across 10 million transactions in September 2026, meaning 40% of volume represents ₹600 crore per month.
At Arvanta's blended fee of 0.20%, monthly processing cost on the ₹600 crore volume in scope is ₹120 lakh.
At Brevis Pay's quoted fee of 0.176%, monthly processing fee for the ₹600 crore volume is ₹105.6 lakh, yielding a gross recurring fee saving of ₹14.4 lakh per month.

After adjusting for the ₹6 lakh/month India-only hosting fee, ₹2 lakh/month higher dispute fees, and ₹4 lakh/month treasury float savings from T+1 settlement, Option B generates a net recurring monthly benefit of ₹10.4 lakh.
Total one-time costs for Option B are ₹65 lakh, comprising ₹40 lakh in migration and engineering costs and a ₹25 lakh early-exit penalty payable under Arvanta's MSA for dropping below 80% volume.
Option B achieves full payback on total one-time implementation costs in 6.25 months.

If phased to avoid Arvanta's ₹25 lakh exit fee, the maximum initial slice is 20% (₹300 crore/month), which delivers a net monthly benefit of ₹2.2 lakh after the fixed ₹6 lakh hosting add-on, dispute delta, and float savings.

Current payment costs are running at ₹36 crore per year against an FY27 budget of ₹33 crore (₹3 crore or 9% over budget); the net annualized savings of ₹1.248 crore from Option B help reduce this budget variance.

Arvanta's counter-offer of an 8% fee cut requires committing 100% volume for 3 years, which would reduce total monthly fees from ₹300 lakh to ₹276 lakh (a ₹24 lakh/month saving) but directly violates Legion's FY27 OKR capping vendor share at 70%.
Payment volume is projected to grow 25% over the next 12 months, which will increase the variable fee savings from Brevis Pay while fixed hosting add-ons remain constant.
Option B enables ₹45 crore/month in cross-border SME pipeline requiring international card acceptance, expected to generate ₹1.08 crore/year in fee revenue.
The Brevis draft agreement allows price changes on 30 days' notice and caps vendor liability at 3 months of fees compared to Arvanta's 12 months, introducing commercial downside exposure.

criterion_scores.reason: Leaves payment costs at an annualized run-rate of ₹36 crore, exceeding the ₹33 crore budget, and forfeits ₹10.4 lakh in net monthly operating improvements.
Yields ₹10.4 lakh net monthly savings after all add-ons and penalties with a rapid 6.25-month payback, though constrained by a ₹25 lakh exit fee and ₹6 lakh/month flat hosting cost.

positions.summary: Option B triggers immediate legal and regulatory violations: Brevis's draft agreement lacks required data localisation, DPA, and RBI audit clauses, while its Singaporean sub-processor Sentrix Risk processes card data abroad in direct breach of Legion policy and RBI mandates. Furthermore, moving 40% of volume breaches Arvanta's 80% volume threshold, incurring a ₹25 lakh early-exit penalty and requiring 90 days' notice.
handoffs: legal: Hand off to infosec to raise a blocking finding regarding Brevis sub-processor Sentrix Risk processing card data in Singapore, violating data localisation constraints (SEC-01, SEC-02).
legal: Hand off to finance regarding the ₹25 lakh early-exit penalty and 90-day notice requirement under the Arvanta MSA triggered by moving 40% volume (LEG-01, LEG-02).
legal: Hand off to customer/ops regarding the 20 settlement complaints breaching the 30-day statutory limit and 900 monthly EMI auto-debit disputes (CUS-03, CUS-10).

claims.text: Moving 40% of payment volume leaves Arvanta with 60%, falling below Arvanta's 80% minimum volume commitment and triggering a ₹25 lakh early-exit penalty before 31 March 2028.
The Arvanta MSA mandates a 90-day written notice period prior to reducing payment volume.

Brevis Pay's fraud-scoring sub-processor, Sentrix Risk Pte Ltd, is based in Singapore and receives card data, directly violating Legion's mandatory policy that payment/card data must be stored and processed only in India.
The draft agreement with Brevis contains no clause stipulating data storage or processing location in India.
The Brevis draft provides no audit or inspection rights for Legion or the RBI, which directly violates RBI outsourcing norms and Legion InfoSec policy.
Arvanta has an executed Data Processing Agreement aligned with the DPDP Act 2023, whereas Brevis has not provided any DPA.

Brevis's contract terms are substantially weaker than Arvanta's: Brevis subjects disputes to Singapore law and arbitration (vs Indian law/Mumbai courts for Arvanta), indemnifies only for 'gross negligence' (vs 'negligence'), caps liability at 3 months of fees (vs 12 months), and permits price changes on 30 days' notice.
Both Arvanta and Brevis are RBI-authorised payment aggregators and support RBI card-on-file tokenisation.

Brevis took 216 hours (9 days) to report an October 2025 security incident to CERT-In, significantly breaching Legion's policy requirement of CERT-In notification within 6 hours and vendor notification within 2 hours.

Arvanta has offered an 8% fee discount on its 0.20% fee schedule in exchange for a 3-year commitment of 100% volume, while its existing contract auto-renews for 2 years unless terminated 6 months before 31 March 2028.

Customer dispute resolution faces regulatory scrutiny, with 20 of 340 settlement complaints (~6%) breaching the 30-day statutory grievance-resolution limit in September 2026, alongside 900 monthly failed EMI debit complaints.

criterion_scores.reason: Fully compliant with Indian law and RBI mandates; has an active DPDP DPA, Mumbai jurisdiction, 12 months liability coverage, and local processing, though settlement grievance resolution limits need operational tightening.

Directly breaches project constraints and RBI norms: offshore processing of card data via Sentrix Risk in Singapore, no contract data localisation clause, missing DPA, lack of RBI audit rights, and severe CERT-In reporting lag history.

positions.summary: Moving 40% of payment volume to Brevis Pay directly fulfills Legion Capital's FY27 vendor-concentration OKR (reducing single-vendor volume from 100% to 60%, below the 70% threshold) and unlocks ₹1.08 crore annually from cross-border SME merchant pipeline deals. Staying with Arvanta perpetuates single-vendor disruption risk, risks merchant churn, and delays strategic product initiatives like Legion Pay Later and cross-border acceptance.
handoffs: legal: Review early-exit fee implications under Arvanta MSA §9.2 (₹25 lakh threshold if volume drops below 80%) versus Arvanta's 3-year exclusivity offer.
ops: Verify routing configurations to ensure overall transaction success rates are preserved across weak issuer banks (Coral Bank and Tamra Bank).
finance: Evaluate net fee impact of Brevis blended fee (0.176%) against Arvanta counter-offer (8% discount on 0.20%) and cost-to-income targets.

claims.text: Legion Capital's FY27 OKR requires that no single payment gateway carries more than 70% of payment volume by 31 March 2027.
Allocating 40% of volume to Brevis leaves Arvanta with 60% of volume, successfully meeting the vendor concentration cap with 6 months remaining before the 31 March 2027 deadline.
Brevis Pay enables international card acceptance, unlocking 30 cross-border SME merchants in the sales pipeline worth ₹45 crore a month in volume.
The cross-border SME pipeline unlocks ₹1.08 crore a year in fee revenue based on a 0.2% take rate on ₹45 crore monthly volume.
70% of lost SME deals in Q2–Q3 FY27 cited lack of international card acceptance, an capability currently supported only by Brevis Pay.
Legion Pay Later (BNPL) is planned for Q1 FY28; Brevis provides native EMI/BNPL APIs whereas Arvanta requires a 4-month custom build.
Brevis checkout offers 11 Indian languages versus 4 on Arvanta, and delivered a 3.1 percentage point mobile conversion uplift during the 2% pilot.
Competitor Vireo Finance migrated to a multi-gateway architecture in June 2026, advertising 99.9% uptime to SME merchants.

Arvanta experienced 3 major availability incidents in the past 12 months, including a June 2026 outage that delayed ₹2.3 crore in collections and forced ₹11 lakh in fee waivers, highlighting single-gateway vulnerability.

Four large merchants generating ₹38 crore a month have threatened exit over settlement delays as merchant churn increased to 2.1% in September 2026, while 2 of Legion's top 5 co-lending partners already settle via Brevis Pay.
Brevis Pay is less mature with 1,200 merchants and 3 years in business compared to Arvanta's 40,000 merchants over 9 years, representing operational scale considerations.
Arvanta offered an 8% fee cut conditioned on 100% volume commitment for 3 years, but accepting this would breach the FY27 vendor concentration OKR and forfeit multi-gateway resilience.

criterion_scores.reason: Fails FY27 vendor concentration OKR (100% single-vendor share vs 70% target), foregoes ₹1.08 Cr/year cross-border pipeline revenue, and delays BNPL launch by 4 months.
Meets concentration OKR (60% Arvanta / 40% Brevis), unlocks ₹1.08 Cr/year international card pipeline, accelerates BNPL roadmap, and matches competitor multi-gateway offerings.

positions.summary: Moving 40% of volume to Brevis Pay significantly improves merchant and borrower experience through faster refunds (3.0 vs 5.2 days), lower latency (1.4s vs 1.9s), higher checkout conversion (+3.1 points), and multilingual reach (11 vs 4 languages), mitigating rising merchant churn (2.1%) and ₹38 crore/month in threatened volume. However, approval must be conditional on routing traffic from Coral Bank and Tamra Bank away from Brevis to avoid severe localized success-rate drops and a 40% surge in customer complaints.
handoffs: legal: 20 settlement delay complaints in September breached the 30-day regulatory grievance limit under Arvanta (CUS-10).
ops: Brevis has inferior routing on Coral and Tamra banks (18% volume) with 94.8%-95.2% success rates and lacks eNACH for 2% of mandates; smart-routing configuration is required (OPS-02, OPS-08).
finance: Brevis charges ₹250 per dispute vs Arvanta's ₹150, creating a ₹2 lakh/month cost delta on 2,000 disputes (FIN-08).

claims.text: Settlement-delay complaints under Arvanta grew 183.33% from 120 in July to 340 in September 2026, driving 20 regulatory breaches of the 30-day limit in September.
Four major merchants represent ₹38 crore per month in volume threatening exit over settlement delays, contributing to monthly merchant churn rising from 1.4% in Q1 to 2.1% in September 2026.
Legion's merchant NPS stands at 41, trailing the industry benchmark of 50, while 22% of 1-star app reviews cite 'payment failed'.
Brevis Pay delivers tangible customer experience advantages, reducing refund turnaround from 5.2 days to 3.0 days and lowering p95 latency from 1.9s to 1.4s.
Pilot results with Brevis showed a 3.1 percentage point increase in mobile checkout conversion and broader accessibility with support for 11 Indian languages versus Arvanta's 4.

UPI AutoPay success is superior on Brevis at 97.4% compared to Arvanta's 96.1%, which will alleviate failed debit complaints; Arvanta currently sees 900 failed EMI auto-debit complaints monthly, with 14% resulting in wrongly charged late fees.
At a support handling cost of ₹180 per ticket, settlement delay tickets alone cost ₹61,200 monthly, and combined with failed EMI complaints cost Legion ₹223,200 per month.
On Coral Bank and Tamra Bank (18% of volume), Brevis payment success drops to 94.8% and 95.2% (vs Arvanta's 97.5%), generating a 40% increase in customer complaints during the pilot.

Arvanta concentration creates severe borrower disruption, evidenced by the 14 June outage delaying ₹2.3 crore in collections and forcing ₹11 lakh in fee waivers across 1,900 borrowers, while competitor Vireo advertises 99.9% uptime with a multi-gateway setup.

Brevis does not support eNACH for two small banks representing 2% of mandates, and its dispute fees are higher at ₹250 versus ₹150 for Arvanta across an estimated 2,000 monthly disputes on the migrated volume.
Brevis enforces MFA and SSO on merchant dashboards, enhancing merchant account security compared to Arvanta's optional MFA.

conditions: Smart-routing rules must keep Coral Bank and Tamra Bank transactions on Arvanta, since Brevis achieves only 94.8%–95.2% success rates and incurs 40% more complaints on those two issuers.
eNACH mandates for unsupported partner banks (2% of mandates) must remain routed through Arvanta.
Brevis dispute escalation SLAs must be tightly monitored to avoid added merchant friction from higher ₹250 dispute fees.

criterion_scores.reason: Staying 100% on Arvanta perpetuates severe settlement delays (340 tickets/mo, 183% growth), regulatory breaches, 5.2-day refund lags, and risks ₹38 crore/mo merchant churn.
Moving 40% volume to Brevis improves refund turnaround (3.0 days), checkout conversion (+3.1 pts), latency, and auto-debit success, provided weak bank traffic is selectively retained on Arvanta.

positions.summary: Brevis Pay directly violates Legion's mandatory data localisation rule and RBI payment aggregator norms by routing card data to Sentrix Risk in Singapore, while omitting contractual data location and audit rights. In contrast, Arvanta Payments maintains fully compliant domestic data handling, signed DPDP-aligned agreements, and timely incident reporting, making Option A the secure and compliant choice.
handoffs: legal: Review and ensure execution of a binding DPDP-compliant Data Processing Agreement and statutory audit clauses with Brevis Pay.
finance: Account for the ₹6 lakh/month recurring cost of Brevis Pay's India-only hosting add-on required to resolve data localisation non-compliance.

claims.text: Legion's information security policy strictly mandates that any vendor processing payment or card data must store and process it solely in India.
Brevis Pay's fraud-scoring sub-processor, Sentrix Risk Pte Ltd, is based in Singapore and receives card data (tokenised card number, BIN, and device data) outside India.
Brevis Pay offers an India-only hosting add-on to keep fraud scoring in Mumbai at ₹6 lakh per month, requiring a 3-week implementation lead time.
The Brevis draft agreement completely omits data location covenants, DPDP-aligned data processing agreements, and statutory Legion/RBI audit and inspection rights.
Brevis Pay has an open high-severity penetration test finding (missing rate limiting on refund API) that has remained unaddressed for 47 days.
Brevis Pay's latest SOC 2 Type II report is 14 months old (period ending 31 July 2025), leaving current operational controls uncertified.

Brevis took 216 hours (9 days) to report an October 2025 data exposure incident to CERT-In, significantly breaching Legion's policy requiring vendor incident reporting within 2 hours and statutory 6-hour CERT-In filing.

Arvanta Payments complies with key governance benchmarks, having reported its minor November 2025 security incident to CERT-In within 5 hours, maintained an active DPDP agreement, and held a valid annual vendor risk assessment.
Both Arvanta and Brevis are RBI-authorised payment aggregators and support RBI card-on-file tokenisation, with Brevis holding PCI DSS v4.0 through June 2027 and Arvanta through February 2027.
Brevis enforces MFA and SSO on merchant dashboards, whereas Arvanta's MFA is currently optional for merchant admin users.
Arvanta is a 9-year-old vendor serving ~40,000 merchants compared to Brevis which is 3 years old with ~1,200 merchants, reflecting higher institutional maturity in security governance.

blocking_findings.fix: Contractually mandate India-only processing in the agreement, activate Brevis's India-only Mumbai hosting add-on, and verify discontinuation of overseas data transfer before any production traffic is routed.

criterion_scores.reason: Arvanta satisfies all core data localisation, CERT-In reporting SLA, and DPDP contractual requirements, though admin MFA remains optional.
Brevis breaches mandatory India data localisation rules, lacks statutory audit and DPDP agreements, has an outdated SOC 2 report, and has an open high pen-test vulnerability.
